codes.sample: 320 senior college students from the College of Teacher Education at a private university in Cebu, Philippines (AY 2024–2025). 252 female (78.75%), 68 male; most aged 20–22. Universal sampling.
codes.ai_system: Artificial intelligence / AI tools in general (academic use)
codes.dependence_measures: Dependence on Artificial Intelligence (DAI) Scale, 5 items, reported as "α and ω=87" (Table 13; aggregate WM 3.12, SD 1.13).

correlations.exposure: Dependence on Artificial Intelligence (DAI) Scale total
correlations.quote: Pearson r at 0.05 level of significance applying the two-tailed test which shows an r-value of -0.005 and p-value of 0.926

codes.possible_duplicate: None found. This may be based on a local thesis by the same authors, but the text does not say so.
codes.note: The only eligible correlate is academic self-efficacy (SSE). Digital competence (SDiCoS) is not an eligible correlate. The DAI is the Dependence on AI scale, 5 items. One item asks about fear of AI replacing skills. The reliability is printed as "α and ω=87", which is probably a typo for .87. The SE–digital competence r = 0.444 is not relevant to this review.

codes.sample: 640 Turkish adults (mostly professionals: teachers, academics, office employees; 56.7% female). Recruited through an online survey; 92.5% used AI tools.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI systems in general (generative AI tools)
codes.dependence_measures: Turkish adaptation of the Generative AI Dependency Scale (Goh et al., 2025). It has 11 items on a 5-point scale and three subscales: cognitive preoccupation, negative consequences and withdrawal. Reliability: total α = 0.91, ω = 0.93.
codes.possible_duplicate: None found. This is a Turkish adaptation of Goh et al. (2025), which used a separate US/Singapore sample.
codes.note: Psychometric validation only (CFA, reliability, invariance). The survey had only demographic/AI-use items plus the GAIDS. Limitations: "no external validation measures were included". No eligible psychological correlate was measured; only demographic and AI-use group variables. OSF data (osf.io/nkdtu) contain no eligible correlates either.

codes.sample: None. This is a narrative literature review with no original data collection.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI, conversational agents and AI tools in general (discussed narratively)
codes.dependence_measures: None administered. The paper describes AI dependency only conceptually (cognitive, academic, decision-making, emotional, productivity and information dependency).
codes.note: Narrative review ("This review examines the relationship between AI dependency and psychological well-being", p.1) with no methods, sample or statistics. Cited primary studies to check: IJETHE 2024 doi 10.1186/s41239-024-00467-0 (n=300); CAEAI 2025, 100381 (n=676); Jia et al. 2025 Behav Sci 15:1348; Internet High Educ 2025, 65, 100978.

codes.sample: 250 Arab adults (Arabic-speaking, recruited on Prolific) who used an LLM almost daily and/or reported relying on it heavily. Mean age 28.27 (SD 6.08); 47.6% male, 52.4% female. A random 50 of them did a retest one week later.
codes.ai_system: LLMs, mostly ChatGPT, then Gemini and DeepSeek ("Primary LLM")
codes.dependence_measures: Arabic LLM-D12 (12 items, 6-point Likert scale), with two subscales: Instrumental Dependency (6 items, α=0.85) and Relationship Dependency (6 items, α=0.90). The total score has α=0.90.
codes.possible_duplicate: The original English LLM-D12 validation (Yankouskaya et al., 2025, ACM TWEB, doi 10.1145/3765895) used a separate UK sample, so it is not a duplicate.
codes.note: Eligible correlates: internet addiction (IAT-7) and ATAI Fear (fear of AI). Only standardised betas from a 5-predictor multivariate regression are reported (Table 4; e.g., IA→Instrumental β=0.271, IA→Relationship β=0.167). There is no correlation matrix or zero-order r. The raw data are on OSF (10.17605/OSF.IO/Q9GZT), so r could be computed from them.

codes.sample: 63 undergraduate students aged 18–25 in Bangalore, India, all with prior AI chatbot experience. Convenience sample recruited online through Instagram and Discord.
codes.ai_system: AI chatbots in general (no specific system named)
codes.dependence_measures: Ad hoc 15-item Emotional Attachment to AI Scale (5-point Likert) on 'emotional reliance, comfort, and perceived connection'. Items reflect emotional closeness, social substitution and normative regard (e.g. 'When there's no one to talk to, I sometimes end up interacting with AI'). No reliability reported. Total: M = 38.90, SD = 11.46.

correlations.exposure: Emotional attachment to AI chatbots (15-item total score)
correlations.correlate_instrument: 8 selected items from the Big Five Inventory (BFI)
correlations.quote: a weak positive correlation between participants' extraversion scores and their emotional attachment scores toward AI chatbots, r (61) = .22, p > .05.

codes.note: Unclear: the exposure is emotional attachment, not clearly dependence. Some items fit emotional reliance or social substitution; normative regard items (e.g. treating AI respectfully) do not. If accepted as emotional dependence, the report is eligible: r with extraversion is in the text (Table 1 is cited but not shown). No other eligible correlates or subscale r.
